section.title: Teach Me to Do Your Will
section.sectionRationale: The last and most theologically weighty of the four Davidic laments closing Book V, counted among the traditional seven penitential psalms, this prayer confesses that no one alive is righteous before God even while pleading for rescue from enemies, and closes by asking not merely for safety but for the Spirit's guidance onto level ground.
section.thesis: David appeals to God's own righteousness and faithfulness rather than his own merit, confessing that no one alive is righteous before Him, and moves from crushing darkness through remembered mercy to an urgent plea that God's good Spirit would both rescue him and teach him to do God's will, safety and holiness sought together rather than safety alone.
section.frameNote: Five movements: a plea for righteous mercy admitting universal sinfulness, verses 1-2; crushing darkness described, verses 3-4; hope revived by remembering God's works, verses 5-6; urgent cries for guidance, verses 7-8; and dependence on God's Spirit for both deliverance and vindication, verses 9-12.

verses.text: O LORD, hear my prayer. In Your faithfulness, give ear to my plea; in Your {{tsedeq|righteousness}}, answer me.
Do not bring Your servant into judgment, for no one alive is righteous before You.

units.label: Crushing darkness
units.note: the weight of pursuit and despair

verses.text: For the enemy has pursued my soul, crushing my life to the ground, making me dwell in darkness like those long since dead.
My spirit grows faint within me; my heart is dismayed inside me.

units.label: I remember the days of old
units.note: hope revived by remembering God's works

verses.text: I remember the days of old; I meditate on all Your works; I consider the work of Your hands.
I stretch out my hands to You; my soul thirsts for You like a parched land. Selah
Answer me quickly, O LORD; my spirit fails. Do not hide Your face from me, or I will be like those who descend to the Pit.
Let me hear Your loving devotion in the morning, for I have put my trust in You. Teach me the way I should walk, for to You I lift up my soul.

units.label: Teach me to do Your will
units.note: dependence on God's Spirit for deliverance and vindication

verses.text: Deliver me from my enemies, O LORD; I flee to You for refuge.
Teach me to do Your will, for You are my God. May Your good {{ruach|Spirit}} lead me on level ground.
For the sake of Your name, O LORD, revive me. In Your righteousness, bring my soul out of trouble.
And in Your loving devotion, cut off my enemies. Destroy all who afflict me, for I am Your servant.

tsedeq.gloss: Righteousness, rightness. David appeals not to his own righteousness, which he denies possessing in verse 2, but to God's own righteous character, His faithfulness to act rightly by His own name and word, the very ground of the psalm's confidence.

ruach.gloss: Spirit, breath, wind. David asks that God's good ruach lead him on level ground, one of the clearest Old Testament pleas for the Spirit's personal, moral guidance, anticipating the New Testament's fuller teaching on the Spirit leading believers into righteousness.

basic.context: Pursued and crushed to the ground by an enemy, David does not appeal to his own righteousness, which he explicitly denies, but to God's faithfulness and righteous character, moving from remembered mercy to an urgent, twofold plea for both rescue and moral guidance.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm describes David's specific crisis of pursuit and near despair; it prescribes the pattern of appealing to God's own character rather than personal merit, of reviving hope through deliberate remembrance of God's past works, and of seeking guidance in righteousness alongside safety rather than safety alone.
basic.originalLanguages: David appeals to God's tsedeq, righteousness, not his own, confessing plainly that no one alive is righteous before God, verse 2. His climactic request asks that God's good ruach, Spirit, lead him on level ground, one of the Old Testament's clearest pleas for the Spirit's personal, moral guidance.
basic.typology: David's confession that no one alive is righteous before God, verse 2, anticipates Paul's citation of similar Psalms texts in Romans 3:10-20 to establish universal guilt, while his appeal to God's Spirit to lead him on level ground anticipates the New Testament's promise of the Spirit's ongoing guidance into truth, John 16:13.
basic.christ: David's plea, do not bring Your servant into judgment, for no one alive is righteous before You, verse 2, finds its answer in Christ, in whom believers are not brought into judgment, Romans 8:1, because His own perfect righteousness is credited to those who trust Him, and His Spirit now leads them, as David asked, into the way they should walk.
basic.god: God is shown as righteous and faithful, hearing prayer not because of the psalmist's merit but because of His own character, personally present to revive, guide, and deliver, and committed to leading His servant not merely to safety but into obedience to His will.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 3:10-20 develops this psalm's confession that no one alive is righteous before God into the doctrine of universal sin. Romans 8:1 answers David's plea not to be brought into judgment, now fulfilled for those in Christ. John 16:13 fulfills the plea for God's Spirit to lead into the right way.
basic.oneStory: David's honest confession that no one is righteous before God, paired with his plea for the Spirit's guidance into right living, anticipates the gospel's full answer, no condemnation for those in Christ and the indwelling Spirit who leads believers, as David asked, on level ground into God's will.

context.literary:
The psalm is bracketed by two matching requests. At the start David asks to be answered 'in Your righteousness' and tells God not to bring 'Your servant' into judgment, verses 1 and 2. At the end he asks again for rescue 'in Your righteousness' and gives the same reason, 'I am Your servant,' verses 11 and 12. Between them the prayer deepens. The frame is a plea made from a place of no merit; the heart of the poem is what David does with his hands, his memory and his thirst.

The word for spirit gives the psalm its inner story. It appears three times. In verse 4, 'my spirit grows faint within me'; in verse 7, 'my spirit fails'; and in verse 10, 'May Your good Spirit lead me.' The psalm travels from a failing human spirit to a good divine one, and the prayer for guidance is not a separate topic added at the end but the answer to the weakness named at the start. Another thread is the root for life. Verse 2 says no one living is righteous, verse 3 says the enemy has crushed 'my life' to the ground, and verse 11 asks God to give life back: 'revive me.' Condemnation, crushing and revival run along one root.

The middle is a quiet turn. Verses 3 and 4 explain why David is crushed, and verses 5 and 6 begin with three verbs of attention: I remember, I meditate, I consider. The last of the three is built on the same root as the 'complaint' of Psalm 142:2, so that the one who poured out his complaint now turns his thought toward God's works. Hands are stretched out, the soul thirsts, and Selah gives a pause. After it, the language speeds up with commands: answer, do not hide, let me hear, teach me, deliver, teach me, revive, bring out, cut off. Prayer has found its voice.
context.historical:
The heading simply says it is a psalm of David. The Septuagint adds a note linking it to the time his son was pursuing him, and the world of the psalm does fit Absalom's revolt, when David left Jerusalem weeping and barefoot, 2 Samuel 15:30, crossed into the wilderness, and arrived with his people 'exhausted,' 2 Samuel 16:14. 'Hungry, exhausted, and thirsty in the wilderness' is how his companions are described in 2 Samuel 17:29. An earlier flight from Saul would also suit the words, so the psalm is best left tied to David's years of being hunted rather than to one event.

Several features make sense against that background. 'The enemy' in verse 3 is singular, a single pursuer who has hunted David's soul, and in verses 9 and 12 the enemies are plural, the pursuer's company. 'Those long since dead' pictures the shadowy existence of Sheol that Israelites dreaded, and the Pit in verse 7 names the same place, as in Psalm 88:4-6 and Lamentations 3:6. In that world, the grave was not merely an ending but a darkness where God's works are no longer recalled, so David's request for God's face has the force of a plea for life.

The request to hear God's loving devotion 'in the morning' fits ancient justice. Kings dealt with the oppressed at the start of the day, and God told David's house to 'administer justice every morning,' Jeremiah 21:12. Absalom had made his pitch in the early morning at the city gate, 2 Samuel 15:2, so there is a bitter irony in David, hunted by that rising son, asking the true King for His morning verdict. The morning is also the time of rescue in the Psalms, Psalm 30:5 and Psalm 90:14.

His confession that no one living is righteous reflects what Israel already knew. Solomon had said in his temple prayer that there is no one who does not sin, 1 Kings 8:46.
context.canonical:
Psalm 143 closes the cluster of laments in Psalms 140 to 143 and takes the sequence from danger to the question of guilt. The church has long counted it as the last of the seven penitential psalms, with Psalms 6, 32, 38, 51, 102 and 130, and it shares its logic with Psalm 130, which asks who could stand if the LORD kept track of iniquities and answers that with Him there is forgiveness, Psalm 130:3-4.

The confession of verse 2 has a long family. Job asks how a mortal can be righteous before God, Job 9:2, and Ecclesiastes says there is no righteous man on earth who does good and never sins, Ecclesiastes 7:20. The New Testament quotes the verse itself. Paul writes in Galatians 2:16 that by works of the law no one will be justified, and in Romans 3:20 that no one will be justified in His sight by works of the law. He is rereading Psalm 143:2, giving it the shape of his argument by adding the words about the law, and the chain of quotations in Romans 3:10-18 draws on this very cluster, since the line about the venom of vipers, Romans 3:13, comes from Psalm 140:3.

The request for the Spirit's leading belongs to a long stream. God gave His good Spirit to instruct Israel in the wilderness, Nehemiah 9:20. Isaiah recalls that the Spirit of the LORD gave them rest as He led them, Isaiah 63:14. David's own prayer after his sin asks that God not take His Holy Spirit from him, Psalm 51:11. The prophets promise that God will put His Spirit within His people and cause them to walk in His statutes, Ezekiel 36:27, and the New Testament says those who are led by the Spirit are sons of God, Romans 8:14.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalm meets a particular temptation in the hunted: to argue one's case by pointing to one's innocence. David could have done that, because he was the wronged party in a political rebellion. Instead the psalm refuses that route. In the second line he forbids himself the plea he might most naturally make, and he puts his case entirely in God's faithfulness and righteousness. First hearers were meant to see that the king of Israel, whose throne depended on God's covenant, still stood before God as a sinner like every other person.

The author also wants his hearers to learn how to rebuild hope when it has gone. David does not talk himself into cheer. He reaches back, remembers the days of old, meditates on God's works, spreads out his hands and admits his thirst. Israel's memory was full of such works, from the exodus to the entry into the land, and the psalm teaches the people to take that memory into their dark times as a living resource, not just a story.

And he wants them to grasp what rescue is for. David asks to be taught to do God's will, and for God's good Spirit to lead him on level ground. He wants to be safe, but he wants to be right even more, because an escape that left him free to walk crooked would not be worth the name. The prayer joins safety and holiness, and a people praying it learn that they are asking to be delivered into obedience, not out of it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm records David's own crisis and his own prayer, but two of its statements are doctrine and not mood. 'No one alive is righteous before You' is not an expression of how David felt that day; the rest of Scripture treats it as the human condition, and Paul rests his case on it. That line is meant to be believed by every reader. By contrast, the pursuit, the darkness and the near despair are David's circumstances, and nothing says that every believer must pass through them or that every plea will be answered by the removal of a human enemy.

The request that God 'cut off' and 'destroy' David's enemies deserves care. It is a prayer, not a command to take up arms, and it is prayed by someone who leaves the matter in God's hands, as the apostle later teaches, 'leave room for God's wrath,' Romans 12:19. Jesus tells His followers to love their enemies and pray for them, Matthew 5:44, so the right use of this verse is not to wish harm on a neighbour but to place injustice before the Judge of all the earth and to rest.

What clearly carries across is the method: appeal to God's character, not to personal merit; remember His works when hope drains away; ask for guidance as well as rescue.

debates.question: How can David ask to be answered in God's righteousness, verse 1, and then say that no one alive is righteous before Him, verse 2?

views.label: God's righteousness is His covenant faithfulness
views.case: Verse 1 sets 'faithfulness' beside 'righteousness,' and verse 11 joins righteousness to 'the sake of Your name.' Here God's righteousness is His loyalty to the promises He has made, which is why David can appeal to it while denying his own.

views.label: God's righteousness is His saving action
views.case: In many Psalms and in Isaiah, God's righteousness is the power by which He rescues and sets things right, Psalm 98:2 and Isaiah 51:5. David therefore asks to be delivered by that righteousness, as one who has fled to God for refuge, verse 9.

views.label: The tension is real and only the gospel resolves it
views.case: Paul reads the verse as exposing a problem that the Old Testament could not solve by itself, how God can be righteous and yet accept sinners. In his reading the answer comes at the cross, where God shows His righteousness 'so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus,' Romans 3:26.

debates.bearing: The first two views describe what the psalm meant for David. The third describes what the psalm waits for. The prayer already has the shape of the gospel: it hopes for mercy on the ground of God's character, and the New Testament shows how that hope is fully met.

debates.question: Does 'Your good Spirit' in verse 10 mean the Holy Spirit as a divine person?

views.label: The Spirit of God, understood in light of later revelation
views.case: Nehemiah 9:20 says God gave His 'good Spirit' to instruct Israel, and Isaiah 63:10-14 speaks of God's Holy Spirit among His people, grieved by rebellion and giving them rest. Read with Psalm 51:11 and Ezekiel 36:27, the verse asks for the very presence of God to lead.

views.label: God's own breath or gracious influence
views.case: Old Testament language about the Spirit is less developed, and the verse could simply ask that God's kindly disposition and power guide David. The psalm says nothing explicitly about personality or Trinity.

views.label: The prayer is for inner renewal in line with the new covenant promises
views.case: Because the verse asks for guidance in doing God's will, some link it to the promise that God would put His Spirit within His people, Ezekiel 36:27. David asks for what the prophets would later announce for all.

debates.bearing: The text itself does not settle personhood, but the New Testament reads this kind of prayer as the Spirit's work, John 16:13 and Romans 8:14. It is fair to say David asked for the presence of God leading him, and we may hear in his words the One whom Jesus later sent.

debates.question: Is the prayer for the enemies' destruction in verse 12 consistent with Jesus' command to love enemies?

views.label: Yes, because it hands judgment to God
views.case: David does not say he will cut off his enemies; he asks God to do it. Romans 12:19 draws the same line, leaving vengeance to God, and the prayer is rooted in covenant justice, since these enemies afflict God's servant.

views.label: It belongs to a stage of revelation that Jesus fulfils and deepens
views.case: Matthew 5:44 asks His followers to pray for those who persecute them. On this reading the imprecation shows a fallen world needing justice, while Christ shows the greater way, praying even for His killers, Luke 23:34.

views.label: Both belong together
views.case: Scripture keeps both a longing for God to end evil and a call to love the evildoer. The final judgment passages, Revelation 6:10 and 20:10, show justice done, while 2 Peter 3:9 shows God's patience for repentance.

debates.bearing: Christians may pray this verse as a cry against injustice and persecution, and as a request that evil be ended, while praying for the person who does evil and leaving the verdict with God.

study.originalLanguages:
The psalm's verbs are precise. In verse 2 'righteous' is a verb, yitsdaq, from the root behind the noun in verses 1 and 11. It is a courtroom word: to be in the right, to be declared just. Job 9:2 asks the same question with the same verb, 'how can a mortal be righteous before God?' The Greek Psalter renders it with the verb for being justified, and when Paul quotes the verse in Galatians 2:16 he keeps that verb and swaps the Hebrew 'living' for 'flesh.' Verse 2 also has the idiom 'enter into judgment,' as in Job 14:3, a trial in which God is the judge and David has no counsel.

In verse 4 'dismayed' translates a verb for being desolated or appalled. It is the verb of Leviticus 26:32, where God lays waste the land so that enemies who live in it are appalled, and of Isaiah 52:14, where many were appalled at the Servant. David's heart has become like a laid-waste place. In the same verse the 'faint' spirit uses the reflexive verb of Psalm 142:3, so the two prayers share the same exhaustion.

The request in verse 8, 'Let me hear Your loving devotion,' uses a causative form: cause me to hear. David cannot generate the word of comfort himself and asks God to speak it, as in Psalm 51:8, 'Let me hear joy and gladness.' The loving devotion is chesed, the covenant love that frames the psalm, appearing again in verse 12 as the ground for dealing with his enemies.

'Level ground' in verse 10 is a phrase built on mishor, a word for level terrain, a plain, and by extension for uprightness. It appears in Psalm 26:12, 'my feet stand on level ground,' and in Psalm 27:11, 'lead me on a level path.' The road he asks for is smooth because it is straight, and the same word can name moral evenness.

Verse 11 asks God to 'revive' him with the verb chayah in its intensive form, the verb of Psalm 119, where the psalmist repeatedly begs, 'revive me,' as in Psalm 119:25. The verb is cousin to the 'living' of verse 2 and the 'life' of verse 3, and the wordplay carries the gospel logic: no living person is righteous, the enemy has crushed my life, and only God can make a life live again. Finally, 'to do Your will' uses ratson, favour or pleasure: what God delights in is to be the pattern of the life.

typology.type: No one alive is righteous before You, verse 2
typology.fulfillment: The verse is quoted by Paul and used to close every mouth, Romans 3:19-20 and Galatians 2:16. The correspondence is between David's confession and the universal verdict of the law. The escalation is that Paul shows where the confession leads: not despair but the righteousness of God, 'apart from the law,' given 'freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus,' Romans 3:21-24. The type falls short only in being a statement of the problem. The psalm sees the lack of any righteous person alive; Christ provides the righteous One.

typology.type: Do not bring Your servant into judgment, verses 2 and 12
typology.fulfillment: David calls himself God's servant and pleads not to be tried. Isaiah later speaks of another Servant who is crushed and who bears iniquity, and who, 'by His knowledge,' will 'justify many,' Isaiah 53:10-11. David's word 'crushing' in verse 3 and the verb of Isaiah 53 are from one root. The servant who deserved the judgment prays to be spared, and the Servant who did not deserve it takes it. The correspondence stops short in one place: David is a sinner pleading for mercy, whereas Christ is the righteous Servant who offers Himself, Romans 8:33-34.

typology.type: Teach me; let Your good Spirit lead me, verse 10
typology.fulfillment: David asks for the guidance that Israel received in the wilderness, when God gave His good Spirit to instruct them, Nehemiah 9:20. The promise of Ezekiel 36:27 sharpens it into an internal gift, and Jesus promises that the Spirit of truth will guide His disciples into all truth, John 16:13. At Pentecost the Spirit fills the believers, Acts 2:4, and Paul says all who are led by the Spirit are sons of God, Romans 8:14. The type falls short because David's prayer was for guidance given to a few; the new covenant gives the Spirit to all who are Christ's.

typology.type: My soul thirsts for You like a parched land, verse 6
typology.fulfillment: The picture of a dry, thirsty land becomes an invitation when Jesus cries out, 'If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink,' John 7:37. The prayer of the thirsty is met in the One who gives living water. The correspondence ends in the last chapter of the Bible, where He gives freely 'to the thirsty' from the water of life, Revelation 21:6. The type is partial: David's thirst is toward a God he cannot yet see face to face, whereas the believer's thirst is now satisfied in Christ and still waits for the final spring.

study.christ:
Psalm 143 states a problem that only Christ solves. David appeals to God's righteousness for an answer and in the next breath confesses that no one living is righteous before God. The tension is not a slip; it is the question of the whole Bible. Paul's answer in Romans 3:21-26 is that God has now shown His righteousness 'apart from the law,' and that He did it in Jesus, whom God 'presented as the atoning sacrifice,' so as to be 'just and to justify the one who has faith.' That final phrase is the exact fit for verses 1 and 2: God remains righteous, and the sinner is not brought into judgment, because the judgment has been borne by another. Romans 8:1 draws the conclusion, and Romans 8:33-34 asks who can bring a charge against God's elect when God is the One who justifies.

The psalm's word 'servant' also leads to a person. David pleads as 'Your servant,' in verses 2 and 12. Isaiah's Servant is the one who is crushed, 'it was the LORD's will to crush Him,' and who 'will justify many,' Isaiah 53:10-11. David is a servant who needs justification; Jesus is the Servant who supplies it. And when the psalmist begs, 'Teach me to do Your will,' he is praying what Jesus can say without qualification: 'I have come to do Your will, O God,' Hebrews 10:7, taking up Psalm 40:8. In Gethsemane He prays 'not what I will, but what You will,' Mark 14:36.

Christ also stands behind the Spirit's leading. He was 'led by the Spirit' in the wilderness, Luke 4:1, and promises that the Spirit of truth will guide His own into all truth, John 16:13. The 'level ground' David could only ask for becomes a road the Spirit now walks with believers.

One should not make every phrase point at Jesus. The darkness 'like those long since dead' is David's description of despair, though it is fair to hear in it a faint foreshadowing of the One who went into death for three days, Matthew 12:40. The strong link is the doctrinal one: the psalm's honest cry is answered where righteousness and mercy meet at the cross.
study.god:
The psalm shows God as the One who answers on the basis of who He is, not on the basis of who we are. David's whole case rests on three attributes named at the start: God's faithfulness, His righteousness and, in verses 8 and 12, His loving devotion. The three are not in tension for him. Faithfulness says God keeps His word, righteousness says He sets things right, and loving devotion says He does so out of covenant love. The prayer assumes that these cannot be pulled apart.

The psalm also shows that God judges and yet hears. The line 'Do not bring Your servant into judgment' acknowledges that God is a judge before whom no one stands, as the rest of the Bible teaches, Psalm 130:3. And yet David believes that this same judge is the refuge to whom he flees, verse 9. Few lines in Scripture hold God's holiness and mercy as close together. The doctrine of God that results is not a compromise between severity and kindness. It is one God whose righteousness includes the rescue of His servant.

God is shown as teacher and guide. 'Teach me the way I should walk' and 'Teach me to do Your will' place Him in the role of the One who instructs, as in Psalm 32:8, 'I will instruct you and teach you the way you should go.' The good Spirit who leads on level ground adds the idea that guidance is not only information but a personal presence, one that brings the traveler to a straight path. Psalm 25:8 says He shows sinners the way, which is exactly who David is.

God is shown as the one who revives. He is the source of life not only in the sense of preserving breath but in the sense of restoring a person who has been crushed and made to dwell in darkness. The revival is asked 'for the sake of Your name,' which means that God has His own reputation bound up in the rescue of those who trust Him, as Psalm 23:3 says of the shepherd.

For worship, the psalm gives permission to pray without a claim. Hands are stretched out, the soul is parched, and the only thing offered is the confession that we have nothing to offer. God receives such a prayer.

crossReferences.note: Paul's use of Psalm 143:2. He says no one will be justified in God's sight by works of the law, adding the law to the psalm's 'no one alive.' The verse shows that the psalm's confession was read as a universal verdict, and that its answer lay in what God had yet to reveal.

Paul says 'by works of the law no one will be justified,' and in the Greek this keeps the verb of the psalm's Greek version. It shows how the early church read verse 2 as the ground of the doctrine of justification by faith.

The answer to the tension in verses 1 and 2. God shows His righteousness at the cross so as to be just and to justify the believer. David asked for an answer in righteousness while denying his own, and Paul shows where the answer comes from.

Asks who could stand if the LORD kept track of iniquities, and answers that with Him there is forgiveness. It is the closest companion to verse 2, and together the two psalms hold the conviction of sin and the hope of pardon side by side.

'How can a mortal be righteous before God?' Job uses the same verb as verse 2 for being in the right. The echo shows that this question was alive in Israel long before Paul, and that suffering sharpened it.

Israel's confession says God gave His good Spirit to instruct them in the wilderness. It is the nearest parallel to verse 10 and shows that the request for the Spirit's instruction rests on what God had already done for His people.

'Teach me Your way, O LORD, and lead me on a level path, because of my oppressors.' The same pairing of teaching, level ground and enemies shows how David linked guidance with pursuit, and how a safe road is also a straight one.

God promises a new heart and His own Spirit within, to cause His people to walk in His statutes. It reads like the answer to verse 10: David asked God's Spirit to lead him, and Ezekiel announces that God will place the Spirit within His people.
The Servant is crushed and will justify many. It answers the psalm's two uses of 'servant' and its worry about judgment: the One who bears iniquity is the one who makes others righteous.

'I will remember the works of the LORD' and 'reflect on all You have done' is the same medicine as verse 5. Together they show that deliberate remembering is a recognised discipline in Israel's prayer when feeling fails.
'All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.' This is the New Testament's answer to 'May Your good Spirit lead me.' The guidance David wanted is now the mark of every child of God.

'He has made me dwell in darkness like those dead for ages' nearly repeats verse 3. The overlap shows how a recognised language of lament carried suffering across generations, and Lamentations too turns from darkness toward hope in the LORD's mercies, 3:22-23.

study.oneStory:
The psalm lives in the world after Genesis 3. 'No one alive is righteous' is the verdict of the fall, and the enemy who has crushed David's life 'to the ground' echoes the sentence that man will return to the ground from which he was taken, Genesis 3:19. The 'darkness' of verse 3 and the 'Pit' of verse 7 are the landscape of that curse. David's cry is therefore not a private mood but the cry of a fallen race seeking the God who made it.

The psalm looks back for its remedy. 'I remember the days of old' points to the exodus and the wilderness, when God gave His good Spirit to instruct His people and led them like cattle going down to the valley, Nehemiah 9:20 and Isaiah 63:11-14. Redemption in Scripture is always remembered redemption, and David teaches Israel to build on what God has already done.

The psalm also looks forward. The promise of a new covenant reaches the very things David asked: God writes His law on the heart and puts His Spirit within, and all will know Him, Jeremiah 31:33-34 and Ezekiel 36:26-27. At the cross the question of how God can be righteous and justify sinners is answered, Romans 3:26, and at Pentecost the Spirit is poured out, Acts 2:4. The church, taught by the Spirit, is the people who have been given what David could only ask for.

The story's end completes the prayer. The thirsty are given water freely from the spring of life, Revelation 21:6, and never again will they hunger or thirst, Revelation 7:16-17. The uneven ground becomes a plain, Isaiah 40:4, a world where righteousness dwells, 2 Peter 3:13, and where the night is gone, Revelation 22:5. The servant who asked not to be judged is welcomed home, and the enemy who hunted him is no more.

sermon.title: How to Argue with God
sermon.why: Piper works through Psalm 143 verse by verse, showing what David wanted, how he prayed, and how he argued his case before God on the basis of God's own righteousness and name rather than his own merit, directly expounding this passage's central logic.

quiz.q: On what basis does David ask God to answer him in verse 1?

options.text: God's own faithfulness and righteousness, not David's personal merit.
options.note: David explicitly appeals to God's character, in Your faithfulness, in Your righteousness, rather than his own worthiness.

options.text: David's flawless record of obedience to God's law.
options.note: Verse 2 explicitly denies any such flawless record, confessing that no one alive is righteous before God.

options.text: The size of David's army and political power.
options.note: The appeal is entirely to God's character, not to any human strength or power.

options.text: A formal legal contract David had drawn up with God.
options.note: The appeal is relational and covenantal, resting on God's revealed character, not a formal contract.

quiz.q: What does David confess about humanity in verse 2?

options.text: That no one alive is righteous before God.
options.note: This blunt confession of universal sinfulness grounds the psalm's appeal to grace rather than merit.

options.text: That some people are righteous enough to earn God's favor.
options.note: The verse states plainly the opposite, that no one alive is righteous before God.

options.text: That only his enemies are sinful, while he himself is blameless.
options.note: David includes himself, asking God not to bring Your servant into judgment, in this universal confession.

options.text: That righteousness is impossible even for God to define.
options.note: The verse concerns human unrighteousness before God's standard, not any ambiguity in God's own righteousness.

quiz.q: How does David revive his hope in verses 5-6?

options.text: By deliberately remembering the days of old and meditating on all God's works and the work of His hands.
options.note: David actively recalls God's past faithfulness as the means of reviving present hope amid despair.

options.text: By ignoring the past entirely and focusing only on his own present feelings.
options.note: The passage describes intentional remembrance of the past, not avoidance of it.

options.text: By seeking advice from foreign kings.
options.note: David's hope is revived through remembering God's works, not through consulting other rulers.

options.text: By convincing himself that his troubles were not really that serious.
options.note: David does not minimize his troubles; he reorients hope through remembering God's faithfulness while still describing genuine distress.

quiz.q: What twofold request does David make in verses 9-10?

options.text: Deliverance from his enemies and instruction to do God's will, led by God's good Spirit.
options.note: David seeks both safety and moral guidance together, not safety alone.

options.text: Only wealth and comfortable living, with no concern for obedience.
options.note: The request explicitly includes, teach me to do Your will, moral guidance alongside safety.

options.text: Only revenge against his enemies with no request for guidance.
options.note: While enemies are mentioned, verse 10 explicitly requests guidance in doing God's will, not merely revenge.

options.text: A request to be left alone by both God and his enemies.
options.note: David actively seeks God's presence and guidance, not distance or isolation from God.

quiz.q: How does this psalm's confession of universal unrighteousness connect to the New Testament?

options.text: It anticipates Paul's teaching that no one is righteous before God and that in Christ there is now no condemnation for those who trust Him.
options.note: Romans 3:10-20 and Romans 8:1 develop exactly this psalm's confession and its resolution in Christ.

options.text: It has no relationship to New Testament teaching on sin and grace.
options.note: Paul directly draws on similar Psalms texts to build his doctrine of universal sin and grace in Christ.

options.text: It suggests that only Gentiles, not Israelites, are unrighteous before God.
options.note: The confession is universal, no one alive, not limited to any single people group.

options.text: It implies that David alone, uniquely among all people, was righteous.
options.note: David explicitly includes himself as a servant needing mercy, not an exception to universal unrighteousness.

questions: David appeals to God's righteousness and faithfulness rather than his own merit. Where are you tempted to approach God on the basis of your own performance rather than His character and grace?

David feels crushed to the ground and dwelling in darkness, yet still turns to prayer. What crushing weight are you carrying right now that needs to be honestly brought to God rather than carried alone?
David deliberately remembers God's past works to revive present hope. What specific past evidence of God's faithfulness in your own life could you deliberately recall this week?

David asks not only to be rescued but to be taught God's will and led by God's Spirit on level ground. Are you seeking safety alone from your current difficulty, or also asking God to shape your character through it?

David confesses that no one alive is righteous before God, yet still boldly asks for mercy. How does knowing that Christ answers this exact confession, no condemnation for those in Him, change how you approach God today?

translationNotes.note: No one alive is righteous before You is one of the Old Testament's clearest statements of universal human sinfulness, later drawn on by Paul in Romans 3:10-20 to establish that all have sinned.

The Pit renders a Hebrew word, bor, that can mean both a literal cistern or grave, and figuratively Sheol, the realm of the dead, the same word used of literal cisterns turned into prisons, Jeremiah 38:6.
I flee to You for refuge carries a footnote alternate rendering, in You I take cover, both expressing David's total reliance on God rather than his own strength for protection.
